Past Most Splats the oldest fade out; a splat drips off when an exit moves over it or its ring breaks. Deterministic: seeds, links and Find Simulation include it.
Controls.splatSizeTip: A splat’s size as a multiple of the ball’s (0.5–2 on the slider).
Controls.splatMaxTip: How many splats stand at once; past it the oldest fade out (10–300 on the slider).
Controls.splatGrowNote: In Grow the splats only paint the ring – the ball grows to fill it.
Controls.ogDesc: Thousands of orbs, each bouncing straight up and down on its own spot. One property varies across the field, so the whole set becomes a wave – it rises from a corner, funnels into the centre or ripples in rings, falls into phase and dissolves again.
Controls.ogColumnsTip: Orbs across the field. Columns × rows is the orb count the clip shows (33 × 33 = 1089). No upper limit: type any whole number.
Controls.ogRowsTip: Orbs along the field. 70 × 70 makes 4900 orbs; past 250,000 a run builds the largest field that fits in memory.
Controls.ogArrangementTip: How the orbs stand: a square grid, a disc of concentric rings, octagon rings or a hex grid. The ring arrangements place columns × rows orbs ring by ring.
Controls.ogVariedTip: What differs from orb to orb: how bouncy it is, how high it starts, when it is let go, its size, its gravity – or its period (perfectly elastic orbs that never settle).
Controls.ogDistributionTip: How the property spreads over the field: at random per orb (from the seed), corner to corner, centre outwards, by rows or columns, in a spiral, in ripple bands or as a checkerboard.
Controls.ogSpreadTip: How far the property ranges across the field. At 0 every orb is alike and the whole field bounces as one.
Controls.ogReleaseTip: When the orbs are let go: all together, ring by ring from the outside in or from the inside out, row by row, or in random slots.
Controls.ogStaggerTip: Seconds between two release steps (rings, rows or random slots).
Controls.ogDropHeightTip: How high the orbs start above the slab, in field widths.
Controls.ogOrbSizeTip: Orb diameter as a share of the spacing: at 100% neighbours touch.
Controls.ogBouncinessTip: How much of its speed an orb keeps at each landing (0.9 = 90%). A varied bounciness spreads around this value; 1 or more never settles.
Controls.ogResolveTip: Tunes every orb's timing a little (its bounciness stays) so that at one moment every moving orb lands at once – the pattern falls into phase, then dissolves again.
Controls.ogElevationTip: How far above the slab the camera looks down from, in degrees: low for a sweeping wave, 90° straight down.
Controls.ogRotationTip: Turns the field around its centre, in degrees.
Controls.ogOrbitTip: The camera slowly circles the field on the simulation clock, so a found run and its export look the same.
Controls.ogFloorTip: Under the orbs: a slab with a grid over a blue grid floor, a round dark plate, the grid alone, or nothing.
Controls.ogMaterialTip: Glossy (a bright highlight and a darker rim), chrome-like metallic, soft matte or see-through glass.
Controls.ogPaletteTip: Colours by current height (a rainbow from green to purple), by ring, by row, in the Ball Colour, or a rainbow by position.
Controls.ogHudTip: Shows the line “1089 bouncing orbs” at the top of the clip.
Controls.ogSoundTip: Notes: a soft tone per landing (a row or a ring lands as a chord). Sleep: very soft, long and low. Music: the landings compose a melody on your scale. Metal: bright clinks. Silent: nothing.
Controls.ogRunSettles: every orb at rest after about {seconds}s
Controls.ogRunNever: never settles – the clip ends the run
Controls.ogFull: Orbs in a run: {count} – the most one run holds ({requested} asked for).
Controls.ogPresetsTip: Fields after the most-liked orb clips: one click switches to Bouncing Orbs and loads the field, the look and the sound.
Controls.flDesc: Fighters from games, comics, shows and movies duel in an arena with their weapons and one ability each. Pick a matchup or your own fighters – a random slot is picked by the seed – and the last one (or team) standing wins.
Controls.flPresetTip: A ready-made matchup in its genre: it picks the fighters and the match type.
Controls.flMatchTip: A 1v1 duel, 2v2 (fighters A+B against C+D, no friendly fire) or a free-for-all of three or four fighters.
Controls.flFightersTip: Every slot's fighter, grouped by division. Random lets the seed pick one – Find Simulation then searches the matchup too.
Controls.flRandomHint: Picked by the seed from the whole roster.
Controls.flRandomHintDivision: Picked by the seed from the first fighter's division.
Controls.flSameDivisionTip: A random slot picks from the division of the first fighter chosen, so a matchup stays in its genre (Marvel vs Marvel, Star Wars vs Star Wars).
Controls.flHpTip: Every fighter's hit points (a fighter's row may give it a little more or less). Type any number from 1.
Controls.flTimeCapTip: After this many seconds the side with more HP left wins (equal HP is a draw). 0 = no cap: the fight goes on until a KO.
Controls.flArenaTip: A square or a circle, inset in the exported square under the names and above the ability boxes.
Controls.flHudTip: The names, the VS card, the ability boxes and the stat lines. Off: just the fight, its effects and the winner banner.
Controls.flHandicapsTip: Every fighter's multipliers of speed, damage, attack speed and cast speed (1 = as in the roster): rebalance a matchup or stage a buff – any number from 0.05.
Controls.lcDesc: Columns of blocks line the arena's wall and every competitor's balls bounce around inside: a hit on a column takes its top block, and every 8th block a competitor takes adds one more ball of its colour. The most blocks wins.
Controls.lcPresetTip: Load a ready-made battle: its rule, its wall, its competitors (a roster of countries) and the clip length.
Controls.lcRuleTip: What a hit on a column does to its top block.
Controls.lcHintKnock: The top block flies off in the hitter's colour and counts for it; a column knocked bare is just wall. The battle ends when every block is gone.
Controls.lcHintClaim: The top block stays where it is, painted in the hitter's colour; a column hands out its blocks from the top down. The battle ends when every block is claimed.
Controls.lcHintSteal: Like Claim, and a hit on a claimed column flips its top block that is not the hitter's – land sways back and forth until the duration runs out.
Controls.lcArenaTip: The shape of the wall the columns stand on.
Controls.lcTeamsTip: How many colours fight for the land – 2 to 12 on the slider, any number typed. The Teams roster names and colours the first ones (up to six), the palette the rest.
Controls.lcRosterNote: The first competitors ({count} of {teams}) take their colours, names and flags from the roster in “Teams & Scoreboard”; the rest come from the palette.
Controls.lcPaletteNote: Palette: {names}… – or set a roster in “Teams & Scoreboard” (its Country picker fills a team with a country).
Controls.lcBallsTip: The balls every competitor starts with.
Controls.lcColsTip: Columns of blocks round the wall, spread over its sides. Any number typed – columns finer than a pixel are drawn as one band.
Controls.lcRowsTip: How many blocks each column holds.
Controls.lcBlockCeiling: A run builds at most {max} blocks: {rows} per column with this many columns.
Controls.lcEveryTip: Every this many blocks a competitor takes add one more ball of its colour at the knock point (0 = never). Steals do not count.
Controls.lcDurationTip: The battle ends here at the latest (a steal battle always does); the clip length follows it.
Controls.lcTitleTip: The title line at the top of the HUD, drawn in capitals.
Controls.lcHudTip: The title, a live bar per competitor (its blocks and balls) and the counters at the top of the video. The verdict banner shows either way.
Controls.lcCaptionNote: A question caption whose answer – the winner – pops in at the verdict.
Controls.lcCaptionAdded: The question is in the Captions section; its answer [winner] names the winner.
Controls.lcRigNote: The Forced Winner is honest steering here: the chosen colour's balls rebound a little more towards land still to take, so it is the favourite, not a certainty. Find Simulation → Winner finds a run it wins.
Controls.teamCountryTip: Fill this team with a country: its name, its flag and its colour

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A ball bounces inside concentric rings that each have a single gap. Every wall it slips through breaks with a satisfying effect. Simple, hypnotic and endlessly rewatchable. Make the exits jump, flee or shrink (Exit Behaviour), or let every hit leave a solid splat of paint (Splat Barrier).

accumulation.name: Accumulation
accumulation.description: The ball has a few seconds to escape before it freezes where it is. Every frozen ball becomes an obstacle for the next one. Will the last ball make it out? Make the exits jump, flee or shrink (Exit Behaviour), or let every hit leave a solid splat of paint (Splat Barrier).

multiply.name: Multiply
multiply.description: Each time a ball escapes the ring it spawns extra balls. The arena fills with bouncing chaos within seconds, which makes for explosive, shareable clips. Make the exits jump, flee or shrink (Exit Behaviour), or let every hit leave a solid splat of paint (Splat Barrier).

lines.name: Lines
lines.description: Every bounce point is connected to the ball by a line, so the run slowly draws intricate string art as the ball ricochets around the circle. With the Splat Barrier on, every wall hit leaves a solid splat of paint.

paint.name: Paint
paint.description: The ball paints a rainbow trail wherever it goes, gradually colouring the whole circle while a live percentage counter tracks the coverage. With the Splat Barrier on, every wall hit leaves a solid splat of paint.

target.name: Target
target.description: Numbered segments line the wall and must be hit in order. Every correct hit triggers a wall-break effect; wrong hits flash red. With the Splat Barrier on, every wall hit leaves a solid splat of paint.

grow.name: Grow
grow.description: The ball is sealed inside one large ring and grows a little with every bounce, filling more and more of the space until there is nowhere left to go. With the Splat Barrier on, every bounce leaves a splat of paint on the ring.

shatter.name: Shatter
shatter.description: Every wall is made of segments with hit points. Each bounce cracks a segment and enough hits shatter it. Clear a path through every wall to escape.

colorMatch.name: Color Match
colorMatch.description: The wall is split into coloured segments and the ball changes colour on every bounce. A segment only breaks when the colours match. Clear them all to escape.

portal.name: Portal
portal.description: Colour-matched portal pairs sit on the wall. Touch one and the ball teleports to its twin. After enough uses the portals burn out and become exits. With the Splat Barrier on, every wall hit leaves a solid splat of paint.

drop.name: Ball Drop
drop.description: Balls of different sizes and weights rain down through rows of pegs and bars, and every hit plays a note pitched by the ball's size. Different gravities fall out of step and the run writes its own polyrhythm.

box.name: Bouncing Shapes
box.description: Squares, circles or DVD-style logos glide through a box at constant speed and every wall hit plays the next note. Big numbers count down with each bounce, logos at speeds in 2:3 or 3:4:5 ratios weave polyrhythms, and a corner hit is the accent everyone waits for.

pendulum.name: Pendulum Wave
pendulum.description: Pendulums tuned so each one swings once more per cycle than the last: the row drifts into travelling waves, splits into groups and snaps back in line every cycle, every crossing a note. Row, arc, circle, galaxy, sliding or bouncing – and a phasing mode that never quite realigns.

polyrhythm.name: Metronomes & Polyrhythms
polyrhythm.description: Up to 400 voices tick at their own tempos – dots orbiting rings in 3:4:5, dots sliding across a circle, a grid of metronomes phasing apart, a spiral – and every tick is a note. They drift into polyrhythms and snap back in phase with a flash and a chord.

collide.name: Collision Playground
collide.description: Hundreds of varied orbs collide in a circle or a box and every collision plays a soft note pitched by size. Make them squishy, drop them in sync, switch the collisions off mid-run or put lollipops on a ring.

glass.name: Glass Smash
glass.description: Gerald is determined to smash all of the glass: he drops down a shaft of glass panes, every landing cracks the pane under him and plays a note, and the last hit shatters it. Stage after stage the glass gets denser and thicker, starts to slide and grows holes – until he rolls through the door marked HOME.

multipliers.name: Multipliers
multipliers.description: Gerald uses the multipliers to get home: balls fall through rows of gates – x2, x3 and x5 clone them, x2 SPEED, x1.5 SIZE and x2 DMG stack with no cap, ÷2 takes half away and release doors let them through in bursts – past bumpers and blockers, while a live counter shows how many make it home.

doublePendulum.name: Double Pendulum Harp
doublePendulum.description: A chaotic double pendulum swings over a harp: every string a bob crosses is plucked and plays its note, while the last bob paints a long rainbow trail. Add pendulums for the butterfly effect, a third arm for a triple pendulum, or let two pendulums spar – every hit a percussive note.

illusion.name: Circle Illusion
illusion.description: Balls sliding on straight lines that secretly roll a circle, rings of bouncing balls rippling in spirals, circles bouncing inside circles with wobbly walls, and balls painting the arena until only a hidden picture stays white – every touch is a note.

stringBattle.name: String Battle
stringBattle.description: Web dominion: every bounce anchors a glowing thread from the ring to the ball, each ball drags a fan of threads, and crossing an enemy's thread cuts it – and costs its owner a life. Numbered lives, a neon moiré style and a finale that gets intense: the last ball standing wins.

powerLayers.name: Power Layers
powerLayers.description: It starts tiny and gets out of control: a white ball bounces between a glowing ceiling and a stack of up to 800 rainbow layers, and every hit destroys as many layers as the power – which then doubles (or follows Fibonacci, the primes, +1, or pure chaos). A new note every level, until the last layer shatters and the ball falls to freedom.

race.name: Square Racing Grand Prix
race.description: Racing squares (or marbles) drop down a long track of pegs, funnels, spinners, pinball bumpers, turbo pads, narrow gates and swap zones that trade two racers' places. Live standings, passing callouts, a podium with confetti – and cups that keep F1 points across races.

battle.name: Square Battle Royale
battle.description: Up to 20 squares with health bars bounce around a box or a circle and smash into each other: the faster square deals the damage, hit squares flash and shrink, and at zero HP they explode with a KO. A shrinking safe zone and heal, shield and speed power-ups keep it tense until the last square standing wins.

ctf.name: Capture the Flag
ctf.description: Two teams of bouncing squares and a base with a flag at each end: touch the enemy flag to carry it, bring it home to score – get tackled on the way and the flag drops where you are. First to the target score, or the better score when the clip ends, wins, with a goal fanfare for every capture.

runner.name: Beat Runner
runner.description: A Geometry Dash-style square runs under a scrolling camera; spikes, pits and blocks sit on the beat of your song, and every real-gravity jump lands exactly on a beat and plays the next note. Auto jump never fails – or play it yourself with Space.

paddle.name: Paddle Keep-Up
paddle.description: Keep the ball up with a platform that slides left and right: every catch is a note, off-centre hits send it sideways with spin, off the walls and the ceiling – until the misses run out and it is game over.

vortex.name: Sound Vortex
vortex.description: Pew! Balls drop into a whirlpool of sound rings and spiral down to the hole in the middle – every ring they sink past plays the next note, so each ball is a rising glissando and the staggered balls weave arpeggios. At the bottom the hole swallows them with a pew and a splash.

journey.name: Journey
journey.description: Gerald bounces through his commute: a column of stages – rings to escape, glass to smash, pegs, multiplier gates, a funnel, a bullseye – one after another while the camera scrolls down, each with its banner and a swoosh, until he walks through his own front door at HOME.

bullseye.name: Bullseye
bullseye.description: BULLSEYE!! Balls fly one after another from a launcher at the top, ping through pegs and bumpers and stick where they land on a dartboard lying at the bottom. Every ring scores, every peg plays a note – and a centre hit pops confetti, a fanfare and slow motion.

beatDrop.name: Beat Drop
beatDrop.description: A ball drops onto planks, blocks, springs, wedges, spinning bars and drum pads that fly in from off-screen just before each beat – so every single landing hits exactly on the beat, with a kick, a snare or the next note of your song.

territory.name: Territory
territory.description: Pong-wars style physics simulation: 2 or 4 teams of bouncing balls paint the tile map their colour, and the live percentage bar tracks who's winning. Vortex VS Bomber – one bounce can flip the board.

maze.name: Maze Escape
maze.description: Who else thought that was blood? Balls drop through a red slot into a seeded, green-glowing maze and bounce their way to the exit, painting every corridor they pass red. Every wall hit is a note that climbs as a ball closes in on the way out – the first ball through the exit wins.

conveyor.name: Conveyor Belt
conveyor.description: Gerald respawns every 3 seconds: a conveyor belt across the top carries ball after ball out of a hatch and drops it into the arena below – concentric rings to escape, a bowl that fills up, or a peg field over bins. Every bounce is a note, the belt hums and clicks, and a counter keeps score: Loaded 17 / Escaped 4.

orbGrid.name: Bouncing Orbs
orbGrid.description: Thousands of glossy orbs on a slab, each bouncing straight up and down on its own spot – 1089, 1936 or 4900 of them. Their bounces vary smoothly across the field, so the whole set rises from a corner, funnels into the centre or ripples in rings, falls into phase and dissolves again, every landing a soft note.

fightLeague.name: Fight League
fightLeague.description: Characters from games, comics, shows and movies duel as balls with their own weapons – swords sweep, hammers fly and come back, guns and wands fire – and every fighter's ability charges up and fires by itself. HP inside the ball; the last one standing wins: Thor vs Loki, Captain Falcon vs Little Mac, Yuumi vs Katarina…

landClaim.name: Land Claim
landClaim.description: Columns of blocks line a square, hexagon or circle arena; colour balls knock the top blocks off, every eighth block spawns another ball, and the most blocks wins – DOMINATION or SUCH A CLOSE BATTLE.

q1.question: Is {siteName} free to use?
q1.answer: Yes: every mode, every customisation option, the sound and Find Simulation – and recording and exporting the videos – with no account to create. Videos made for free carry a small watermark; Pro removes it for $10 a month or $79 a year.

q2.question: What video formats and resolutions can I export?
q2.answer: You can record 500×500 (square), 1280×720 (HD), 1920×1080 (Full HD) and 1080×1920 (vertical, TikTok) clips between 10 and 120 seconds long. Browsers that support MP4 recording export MP4; others export WebM.

q3.question: Can I use the exported videos commercially?
q3.answer: Yes. Everything you create is yours to use on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram or anywhere else, with no attribution required.

q4.question: Do I need to install anything?
q4.answer: No. The whole tool runs in your browser. Open the site and start creating.

q5.question: Can I save my settings?
q5.answer: Yes. Save as many presets as you like to your browser's local storage and load them back at any time. The URL also updates as you tweak settings, so you can bookmark or share a setup.

q6.question: Does it work on mobile?
q6.answer: The simulator is designed for desktop browsers, where there is room for the canvas and the controls side by side. It runs on phones too, but a laptop or desktop is the better experience.

q7.question: Are there keyboard shortcuts?
q7.answer: Yes. Press Space to pause or resume and R to restart the simulation.

q8.question: How do I upload a custom ball image?
q8.answer: Open the Ball & Physics section, enable Show Advanced Options and click Choose Image. Any image works: logos, photos, memes. Or pick an emoji from the emoji grid.

q9.question: How does the custom sound feature work?
q9.answer: In the Custom Sound section, choose a song from the built-in library or import a MIDI file. The melody is extracted from the file and every wall hit plays its next note, turning the run into a musical performance. Prefer a sound effect? Switch Bounce Sound to Audio sample and pick a built-in click, pluck or kick, or upload your own clip – it is pitched per wall and included in the recording.

q10.question: What makes {siteName} a satisfying ball simulator?
q10.answer: The loop is simple: a ball bounces inside rings with tiny gaps, and every time it slips through something rewarding happens: confetti, a shatter, a shockwave. Because you control physics, colours and effects, the tension and the payoff look exactly the way you want.

q11.question: Can I use {siteName} as a satisfying ball clicker?
q11.answer: It is not a clicker game, but it scratches the same itch. You watch, anticipate the gap and get rewarded with effects and sound on every escape. The run plays itself, so it is the satisfaction without the tapping.

Editorial.physicsP1: Every run starts from the same idea: a ball bouncing inside a ring. Speed, gravity and bounciness change how it moves, a bit like dropping a real ball into a bowl and deciding how fast it falls and how hard it ricochets. The engine steps the world sixty times per second with several sub-steps per frame, so collisions stay stable even at high speed.
Editorial.physicsP2: Each ring has a small gap. When the ball lines up with it and passes through, the ring breaks with the effect you picked: confetti, shattering glass or a shockwave. The ball moves on to the next ring, and the process repeats until it escapes or the recording ends.
Editorial.physicsP3: Every mode layers its own rules on top: the ball might split into a swarm, freeze into an obstacle course, or grow with every bounce. All of it runs locally in your browser; nothing is uploaded and the video is encoded on your own machine.
Editorial.modeClassic: A single ball bounces through concentric rings, each with a gap. Break through every wall to escape. The default mode: simple, hypnotic and endlessly watchable.
Editorial.modeAccumulation: The ball has limited time to escape. If it fails, it freezes in place and becomes a new obstacle, and a fresh ball spawns. The arena fills up fast. Can the last one get out?
Editorial.modeMultiply: Each time a ball escapes the ring it spawns extra balls, so one ball quickly becomes a swarm. Great for explosive, chaotic clips that fill the screen.
Editorial.modeLines: Every bounce point is connected to the ball by a line, producing intricate geometric patterns. Part physics, part generative art.
Editorial.modePaint: The ball leaves a colourful trail as it moves, gradually covering the circle. A percentage counter tracks how much you have painted. Try to reach 100%.
Editorial.modeTarget: Numbered segments appear on the wall. Hit them in order; each correct hit triggers a break effect, and wrong hits flash red.
Editorial.modePortal: Colour-matched portal pairs sit on the wall. Touch one to teleport to its twin. After enough uses the portals burn out and the ball breaks free.
Editorial.modeShatter: Walls are split into segments with hit points. Each bounce cracks a segment and after enough hits it shatters. Clear a path through all walls to escape.
Editorial.modeColorMatch: The wall is split into coloured segments and the ball changes colour on every bounce. A segment breaks only when the colours match. Clear them all to win.
Editorial.modeGrow: The ball is sealed inside a single ring and grows with every bounce, taking up more and more of the space until it can barely move.
Editorial.modeDrop: A tall board of pegs and bars instead of rings. Balls of different sizes and weights drop from the top and every hit plays a note, big balls low and small balls high, until they all come to rest – or forever with Rain on.
Editorial.modeBox: A rectangular box instead of rings. Squares, circles or DVD-style logos travel in straight lines at constant speed and reflect perfectly off the walls; every hit plays the next note of the melody or a note that depends on the wall. Each shape carries a big number that counts down per bounce, flashes, grows a little and changes colour, and several logos at speeds in ratios like 2:3 or 3:4:5 weave a polyrhythm until every number reaches zero – or forever with the countdown off. A logo that hits a corner plays a louder note and lights up the screen.
Editorial.modePendulum: No rings: 5–60 pendulums tuned like the classic pendulum wave, so the slowest swings K times per cycle and every next one once more. In line at the start, they drift into travelling waves, split into two and three groups and snap back in line at the end of every cycle; a centre crossing (or an extreme) plays a note pitched by the pendulum's place in the row, and bobs that align play one chord. Six layouts – a row under a bar, an arc of pivots swinging toward the centre, bobs on radii from the centre or on a rotating polygon, a slowly turning galaxy that draws spiral arms, sliders on rails and balls bouncing on a floor – plus a phasing option that turns the tuning into a Reich-style tempo phase shift.
Editorial.tipFindSimulationBody: Rather than guessing, let the tool search for a seed that produces a run of your target length. Open Find Simulation below the canvas, set the duration and let it scan seeds. Once it finds one, the run lasts exactly that long, which makes recording predictable.
Editorial.tipLayerEffectsBody: Rainbow walls, glow, colour trails and wall-break effects stack. Try a reactive background with confetti breaks and a glow; the extra layers keep viewers watching.
Editorial.tipTextHooksBody: Top and bottom overlays give context. A question like "Will it escape?" or a countdown builds anticipation. Adjust the text size so it is readable at a glance on a phone.
Editorial.tipClipLengthTitle: Match the clip length to the platform
Editorial.tipClipLengthBody: Shorter clips (15 to 30 seconds) tend to perform better on TikTok and Reels. Set the duration in the Recording section and pick the vertical 1080×1920 resolution.
Editorial.tipPresetsTitle: Save your favourite setups as presets
Editorial.tipPresetsBody: When a configuration works, save it and load it again for your next video. Consistent series perform well because the audience knows what to expect.
Editorial.tipSpeedBody: Use the 2× to 8× speed buttons to fast-forward through a long run while previewing. Before recording, set it back to 1× so the export captures every frame at full quality.
Editorial.troubleExportQ: The video export looks wrong or is missing frames
Editorial.troubleExportA: Use a recent version of Chrome, Edge or Firefox; recording works best there. Close other tabs and apps to free up memory, and keep the simulator tab visible while it records. Chrome and Safari export MP4; Firefox exports WebM, which every major platform accepts.
Editorial.troubleAudioQ: The simulation does not play audio
Editorial.troubleAudioA: Browsers block sound until you interact with the page. Click anywhere first, then press Start. If there is still no sound, check the system volume and make sure the site is allowed to play audio.
Editorial.troubleSpeedQ: The ball moves too fast or too slow
Editorial.troubleSpeedA: Open the Ball & Physics section and adjust Ball Speed. Lower values are easier to follow; higher values give more energetic clips. Gravity also changes the pacing: lower gravity keeps the ball floating longer between hits.
Editorial.troubleSettingsA: Presets are stored in your browser's local storage. Clearing site data or using a private window removes them. Copy the share link of a setup you care about so you can restore it later.
Editorial.troubleMidiQ: My custom MIDI file does not load
Editorial.troubleMidiA: Very complex files with many simultaneous tracks may not parse. Try a simpler single-melody MIDI (format 0 or 1). The tool keeps only the highest note at each moment, so a lead-melody export from your music software works best.
Editorial.troubleStuckA: Send a note through the feedback page and describe what you were doing.
Editorial.modePolyrhythm: No rings to escape: 2–400 voices each tick at their own tempo and every tick plays a note. Rings (dots orbiting 1, 2, 3… times per cycle and ticking at 12 o'clock, optionally as rotating polygons), arcs (dots sliding along the chords or semicircles of a circle and ticking at both ends), a grid of metronomes, or a spiral whose tick points line up again every cycle. The tempos follow the harmonic series, an arithmetic BPM series (the Reich-style tempo phase shift) or your own ratio list such as 3,4,5,7. The moment every voice ticks together is computed exactly and lands as a chord and a flash; the run ends after the chosen number of cycles and always lasts the same time, so it fits any clip.
Editorial.modeCollide: No rings: 10 to 2000 orbs of different sizes – mass follows size – bounce around a circle or a square and off each other with elastic collisions, under as much or as little gravity as you like. Every collision plays a soft note pitched by the smaller orb (big orbs low, small orbs high, on a pentatonic ladder snapped to your scale), and only the dozen most energetic collisions of each frame sound, so hundreds of orbs sound like rain on glass instead of noise. Variants: squishy orbs that squash on every impact, a sync start that drops them all from a grid at once, an anti-collision switch that lets them pass through each other at a chosen second, and lollipops on a ring that collide along a circular track.
Editorial.modeGlass: The geraldbounces glass format, no rings: a portrait shaft of horizontal glass panes stands between the ball and a doorway marked HOME. The ball falls and every landing cracks the pane below it – a procedural crack grows from the impact point – and plays the next note of your melody or, without one, a scale degree by row; on its last hit a pane shatters into shards with an accented note and a glass-break sound, and the ball crashes through to the next pane. After the last pane of a stage the camera scrolls down to the next one: more panes, thicker glass, panes that slide left and right and panes with holes the ball must miss. The final stage ends with the ball rolling into the doorway and a celebration. Every run is deterministic, so Find Simulation can pick a seed for your clip length.
Editorial.modeMultipliers: A tall board the camera scrolls down, always following the lowest ball. Every row is split into 2–4 gates: count gates (x2, x3, x5) clone each ball that passes – up to a ball cap you choose, from 50 to 2000 –, speed, size and damage gates stack multipliers on it with no upper limit, ÷2 gates absorb every second ball and release gates hold a pile on a door that opens in bursts. Splitter pegs, kicking bumpers, funnels and blockers with hit points (the damage multiplier wears them down faster) sit between the rows, every hit is a note on a pentatonic plinko piano, and the HOME zone at the bottom counts the arrivals live until the final “N Gerald made it home”. A ball that grows wider than the board outgrows it and ends the run with a celebration. Set a target count and Find Simulation looks for a seed whose final count lands within 5 % of it. The same multipliers float as pickup orbs in the ring modes (Ball section → Multipliers).
Editorial.modeDoublePendulum: No rings: one to four double pendulums – or triple pendulums – swing from a pivot in the middle of the video, integrated step by step (an adaptive fifth-order Runge–Kutta scheme whose sub-steps shorten wherever the swing gets violent), so the chaos is real physics and the energy holds for the whole clip. Up to 24 harp strings stand across the playfield, vertical or radial; every bob that crosses one plucks it – the string vibrates and plays its note, tuned to the scale of the Custom Sound section across one to four octaves – while the last bob draws a long rainbow trail. Several pendulums start a hair apart and fly apart after a few seconds (the butterfly effect); sparring hangs two side by side whose bobs collide elastically, every hit a percussive note and a flash. Arm lengths, masses, gravity, friction and the start angles (or a seeded random start) are all adjustable, and the run ends with the clip or never.
Editorial.modeIllusion: No rings to escape: four project.jdm illusions. Lines – N balls each slide back and forth on a diameter of the big circle, ball i at the angle i·π/N with the phase offset i·π/N, so together they form a smaller circle rolling around inside; each ball plays its note when it touches the rim. Rings – concentric rings with one bouncing ball each; the rings turn at different speeds, so the bounces ripple outward in spirals and line up again every cycle. Nested – a circle bouncing inside a circle inside a circle (2–5 layers) with elastic collisions and walls that wobble where they are hit. White spaces – the balls paint the white arena black but bounce off shapes they can never enter, so a hidden picture chosen by the seed is revealed at the end. Everything is deterministic, and the Wobbly Walls slider of the Visual section makes the walls of every ring mode bounce like jelly too.
Editorial.modeStringBattle: The oddplayground WEB DOMINION duel: 2–6 numbered balls bounce inside one thin ring on black, and every wall bounce anchors a glowing thread from the impact point to the ball, so each ball drags a fan of threads behind it (the oldest detach and fade). Cut: crossing an enemy thread snaps it with a pluck and costs its owner a life; Touch: the threads are lasers that burn whoever touches them; Collide: the slower ball of every collision loses a life. A ball at 0 lives shatters like glass and its threads dissolve; when two are left and one is a cut from elimination the finale speeds everything up and the halos strobe, and the last ball standing wins – with slow motion on the final cut when the camera's slow motion is on. The neon style turns the threads into endless lines that paint moiré art across the whole canvas, with a jelly ring and glitch bars. Every seed replays exactly, Find Simulation searches a battle's length or its winner, and a team roster lends the balls its colours and names.
Editorial.modePowerLayers: The oddplayground power-layers format, no rings: a navy portrait playfield with a glowing ceiling bar in its upper third and, from mid-screen down, a dense stack of 20–800 thin rainbow layers – the layers between the ball and freedom. One white ball bounces between the ceiling and the top of the stack with a slight seeded drift. Every impact destroys as many layers as the current power – they shatter into coloured particles and the stack drops – and the power then doubles, follows Fibonacci or the primes, grows by one, or is drawn from the seed (chaos: some hits destroy dozens, others change nothing). Two rainbow pills show the rule, the power and the level, every level plays the next note of your scale, a big hit adds a chord and a whoosh, and when the last layer goes the ball falls through the bottom to freedom. Every bounce takes the same time, so a run lasts the hit count times the bounce period – Find Simulation says so, or searches the chaos seeds for your clip length.
Editorial.modeRace: The project.jdm marble-race format, no rings: 2–16 named racers – the Teams roster's names, colours and emoji – drop from a start grid down a long vertical track generated from the seed. Rows of pegs, funnels, spinners, pinball bumpers, turbo dash pads, narrow gates and swap zones (the first racer through arms one, the second swaps places with it) shuffle the order; every obstacle a racer hits plays its own note, every overtake a rising chime. The camera follows the leader or frames the pack, a mini-map shows the whole track, the standings list positions and gaps, and the finish brings a fanfare, a podium and confetti. Loop the track for several laps, switch on a cup to keep F1 points across races, or pick a staged winner.
Editorial.modeBattle: No rings: 2–20 squares with hit points bounce around a box or a circle and into each other. When two collide, the faster one deals damage in proportion to their closing speed; the square that is hit flashes and shrinks a little, and at 0 HP it explodes into shards with a KO callout. An optional safe zone closes in from the eighth second and pushes the survivors together, and heal, shield and speed power-ups appear at seeded times. The last square standing wins under a banner with confetti. Seeded and deterministic, so Find Simulation can search for a battle of a given length.
Editorial.modeCtf: No rings: two teams of one to four squares play capture the flag in a box with a base and a flag at each end. A square that touches the enemy flag carries it and scores when it reaches its own base; a carrier hit by an enemy drops the flag where it is – the enemy can grab it again, its own team sends it home. The director nudges rebounds toward each square's goal, the scoreboard shows the captures and the clock, and every capture plays a goal fanfare. The first team to the target score wins, otherwise the better score when the clip ends.
Editorial.modeRunner: The project.jdm "realistic gravity in Geometry Dash" rhythm runner, no rings: a square runs along a floor at a constant speed under a scrolling camera. The course is planned on the beat of the loaded song (its detected beat – the same detector as Picture Paint) or of the BPM: for every obstacle – a row of spikes, a pit, a block to jump onto and later drop off – the jump solver takes the flight time of a jump under real gravity with a fixed take-off speed and times the take-off so that the landing falls exactly on a beat. With Auto Jump the square jumps at those times and never fails; without it you jump with Space and a crash restarts the section. Every landing plays the next note with a puff of dust; the finish plays a chord.
Editorial.modePaddle: The "Ball Bounce Game with Moving Platform" format, no rings: a ball falls under real gravity onto a platform that slides left and right; a catch launches it back up – higher from the centre, lower and sideways with spin from the edges – so it wanders off the walls and the ceiling, and every catch plays the next note. The auto controller predicts every landing and heads there; its Skill decides how often it arrives early or late, so the misses (and the game over after the allowed ones) are deterministic for a seed. Or move the platform yourself.
Editorial.modeVortex: The geraldbounces "sound vortex, pew" format, no rings to escape: a whirlpool seen from above – a funnel of 6–24 concentric sound rings over glowing spiral arms, with a hole in the middle. One ball after another enters at the rim with a sideways speed and spirals inward under a central pull that grows toward the centre, plus a little drag; it takes the Spiral Time to reach the hole, whirling faster and faster on the way. Every ring it sinks past plays the next note of your scale – melody, instrument, hit sample and beat lock included – so each ball is a rising glissando and the staggered balls weave arpeggios. The hole swallows it with a pew, a fast downward pitch sweep, and a splash; with the loop on it comes back at the rim. The balls shrink with depth for a 3-D feel, and every run is deterministic, so Find Simulation can pick a seed for your clip length.
Editorial.modeJourney: The geraldbounces commute format – "Gerald bounces through his commute", "let him out!": a column of stages the ball clears one after another while the camera scrolls down. Rings is a compact Classic escape (3–9 rings with rotating gaps; the ball drops down a chute into the core), Glass a few Glass Smash panes that crack on every landing and shatter, Pegs a Ball Drop peg field whose rows play a rising scale, Multipliers two or three rows of gates (x2 DMG, x1.5 SPEED, x1.25 SIZE) that power the ball up for the rest of the trip, Funnel a converging funnel, Bullseye a landing target that scores 10–100 before its trapdoor opens, and HOME the doorway with confetti and the total time. Every stage change shows a banner and plays a swoosh, a mini-map beside the column shows how far Gerald has come, and every note goes through your instrument, scale, beat lock, hit samples and melody. Build the route in the Journey block (sizes, order, add and remove) or let the seed draw a random one; every run is deterministic and always reaches HOME, so Find Simulation can pick a seed for your clip length.
Editorial.modeBullseye: The geraldbounces "bulleye!!" format, no rings to escape: a portrait field with a dartboard target – 3–10 concentric rings in dartboard colours – lying at the bottom. A launcher at the top fires 1–30 balls one after another through a short field of pegs and bumpers (Chaos decides how many stand in the way). The ring a ball lands in scores – 10 for the centre, less further out, nothing off the target – with a popup and a running total, and the ball sticks where it landed, so later shots can bounce off earlier ones. Pegs play notes of your scale like a keyboard from left to right, landings thud lower the further out they are, and a centre hit is a BULLSEYE! with confetti, a fanfare and half a second of slow motion. The target can slide left and right, a rigged Perfect Shot is steered into the bull, and the final banner shows the total and the best shot. Seeded and deterministic, so Find Simulation can search for a run of your clip length.
Editorial.modeBeatDrop: A rhythm mode without rings, made for music edits: a portrait scene on a dark gradient where one ball drops and bounces from obstruction to obstruction, and every obstruction flies in from off-screen – from the left, the right, the top or the bottom, never from the side the ball comes from – with a smooth ease and settles a hair before its beat, so the ball lands on it exactly on the beat. The run is planned ahead from the beat it follows (the loaded song's detected beat, or the BPM setting): the take-off speed of every flight is solved so the flight takes exactly the time between two beats, at any tempo and on irregular grids, so every landing is within a fraction of a millisecond of its beat. Six kinds of obstruction – planks, blocks, spring pads (a higher bounce with a boing), wedges (they send the ball sideways), spinning bars (flat exactly at the beat) and big drum pads – squash on impact, glow with the beat and slide away with a fade once the ball has left; the ball squashes and stretches and leaves a motion trail, and every landing throws a ripple and a puff of particles. Landings play synthesised drums – a kick on beats 1 and 3, a snare on 2 and 4, hats on the off-beats, plus each obstruction's own accent – the next note of the melody, or both. Endless scrolling follows the ball down forever; the arena keeps it inside the view. It can never miss a beat, so Find Simulation just picks a seed and times the clip to the beats it covers.
Editorial.modeTerritory: The oddplayground pong-wars battle: a tile map split into 2 or 4 team regions, every team's balls bouncing inside its own colour. A ball passes through tiles of its own colour and bounces off any other, converting the tile it hits – so every bounce pushes the border, and the live percentage bar under PICK A SIDE swings with it. Every team can have a power: the vortex curves its path and drags a whirl whose spiral arms convert enemy tiles, the bomber arms every few seconds and blows on its next bounce off an enemy tile, taking every tile within its reach (with a shock ring, debris and a jolt of the board), the painter dashes straight through enemy territory painting a trail, and the ghost passes through enemy tiles and converts a 3×3 block on every wall bounce. The balls collide with each other, the optional dotted grid deflects them, the last five seconds speed everything up, and when the countdown runs out the team with the most tiles wins – with slow motion when the lead flips in the finale and the camera's slow motion is on. Every seed replays exactly, Find Simulation searches for a run your chosen team wins, the Forced Winner rigs one, and a team roster lends the teams its colours and names.
Editorial.modeMaze: oddplayground's maze reels (“who else thought that was blood”): a seeded perfect maze with glowing green walls on near-black – a red entrance slot in the top wall and an exit gap in the bottom wall. 1–8 balls drop in one after another and work their way through physically (a downward pull, perfectly elastic walls), steered by a brain: pure bounce, a wall follower or an explorer that prefers the corridors it has not visited. Every cell a ball passes is painted red, every wall hit is a note that climbs as the ball nears the exit, and the first ball out wins – with a distance-to-exit bar per ball in the HUD and optional fog over the unvisited cells for suspense. Find Simulation times the run or picks the winner.
Editorial.modeConveyor: A conveyor belt runs across the top of the field and drops a ball into the arena below every few seconds – Gerald respawns, again and again. Pick the arena: concentric rings with rotating gaps that every ball has to escape on its own (the rings never break, and a second belt carries the escaped balls out of the field), a bowl that fills up until it spills over, or a peg field that sorts the balls into bins. Freeze on Landing turns every ball that lands into an obstacle for the next one, so the pile grows; Variety mixes sizes and colours. Every bounce is a note of your scale, the belt hums and clicks, and the counter keeps score – Loaded 17 / Escaped 4. In Classic and Multiply the same respawn timer drops in a new ball every few seconds. Seeded and deterministic, so Find Simulation can pick a run of your clip length.
Editorial.modeOrbGrid: A field of orbs – a square grid, a disc, octagon rings or a hex grid, 33 × 33 = 1089 by default and no upper limit – seen in perspective on a slab or a round plate. Every orb bounces straight up and down on its own spot, and one property varies across the field: bounciness, drop height, release delay, size, gravity or period, spread corner to corner, centre outwards, by rows, in a spiral, in ripple bands or at random. The orbs drift in and out of phase, so the field becomes a rising sheet, a funnel or rings – and with Resolve Moment on, every moving orb lands at once before the pattern dissolves. Colour them by height, make them glossy, metallic, matte or glass; every landing is a soft note (a row lands as a chord), or a sleep sound, a melody composed by the bounces or metal clinks. The run ends when every orb is at rest, so Find Simulation can pick a run of your clip length – or one still bouncing when the clip ends, or one that falls into phase at a chosen second.
Editorial.modeFightLeague: Fighters from video games, comics, TV shows and movies – Thor, Loki, Captain Falcon, Little Mac, Yuumi, Katarina and fifty-odd more, grouped into divisions so a matchup stays in its genre – duel as balls in a square or round arena. Every fighter carries its own weapon, drawn as a simple vector silhouette: swords sweep on every bounce, hammers fly at the foe and come back, fists punch, guns, bows and wands fire, breath and beams burn. A hit takes HP – the number inside the ball and the bar under it – knocks the foe back and charges the ability meter in the box at the bottom; when it is full, the ability's name flashes for 0.4 s and it fires by itself: lightning, decoys, beams, chokes, shockwaves, summons, bullet time. Play 1v1, 2v2 or a free-for-all; the last fighter or team standing wins, or the side with more HP at the time cap. Seeded and deterministic: Find Simulation finds a run A or B wins, a double KO or a fight of your clip length – and the Forced Winner rigs it.
Editorial.modeLandClaim: A land-claim battle: columns of blocks stand on the inside of a square, hexagon or circle wall, and two or more competitors – a Teams roster of countries gives them their flags, names and colours – bounce their balls around inside at a constant speed. Under the knock rule a ball that hits a column takes its top block: the block flies off in the hitter's colour and counts for it, and every eighth block a competitor knocks adds another ball of its colour at the knock point, so a lead snowballs into a swarm. The claim rule paints the blocks where they stand instead, and the steal rule lets a hit take a rival's block back – the land sways until the clock runs out. The battle ends when the wall is taken or at its duration, and the most blocks wins: DOMINATION past 60% of the land, SUCH A CLOSE BATTLE when the top two are within 5%. Every seed replays exactly, Find Simulation searches for a chosen winner, a close battle or a run that ends at a chosen second, and the Forced Winner favours a colour by aiming its rebounds at the land still to take.

TikTokBallVideos.title: Bouncing Ball Videos for TikTok
TikTokBallVideos.p1: Bouncing-ball simulations are one of the most dependable formats on TikTok. The premise is tiny, a ball trapped inside rings with narrow gaps trying to bounce its way out, but the payoff is satisfying enough to hold attention for a whole short-form clip. {siteName} is a browser tool built for exactly this kind of content: its physics controls, visual effects and one-click vertical export are free, and Pro takes the watermark off the videos.
TikTokBallVideos.p2: What makes the format work is its built-in tension arc. The ball ricochets faster, the walls close in, the gap looks impossibly small, and then the ball slips through and everything pays off with confetti, a shatter or a shockwave. That loop fits naturally into 15 to 60 seconds, which is where TikTok engagement peaks.
TikTokBallVideos.p3: TikTok rewards videos that hold viewers to the end and get replayed. Ball physics does both: people stay to see whether the ball escapes and rewatch to catch the effects they missed. The format also fits TikTok's sound culture: {siteName} can play a melody note by note on every wall hit, turning the physics into a musical performance.
TikTokBallVideos.p4: There is no dialogue, no face on screen and no setup. Just a clean visual hook that works even as background noise for a scrolling viewer, which is why the format regularly out-performs more produced content in the discovery feed.
TikTokBallVideos.p5: TikTok's preferred aspect ratio is 9:16 vertical, 1080×1920 pixels. {siteName} records directly at that size, so there is no cropping, no re-encoding and no external editor. Set the recording duration (10 to 120 seconds), press record and download a platform-ready clip.
TikTokBallVideos.p6: You can also export 500×500 (square), 1280×720 (HD) or 1920×1080 (Full HD) for Reels, YouTube Shorts and other platforms. Recording happens entirely in your browser and nothing is uploaded. Videos made for free carry a small {siteName} watermark, which Pro removes; your own custom watermark is optional.
TikTokBallVideos.p7: The best TikTok ball videos follow a simple recipe: a clear visual hook in the first second, a visible progress indicator such as the number of walls left, and a satisfying payoff when the ball finally escapes. The Find Simulation tool searches for a seed that produces a run of your target length, so you can plan the clip instead of guessing.
TikTokBallVideos.p8: Every mode, from Classic and Multiply to Ball Drop, Square Racing and Glass Smash, produces a different rhythm, so you can vary your content without starting over. Save your favourite setups as presets and post a new video every day with one click.

About.title: About {siteName}
About.p1: {siteName} started with a simple frustration. Bouncing-ball physics videos were everywhere, pulling in millions of views, and every way of making one was clunky: learn a game engine, pay for an app, or repost a clip a thousand other accounts had already used. None of that suited someone who just wanted to make a good video and post it. So we built the tool we wished existed: open a tab, make the video, download it, done.
About.p2: That idea still runs the whole site. {siteName} is free, works in your browser and asks nothing of you before you start. No sign-up and no install: every mode and setting is yours to play with, and so is the video export – free videos carry a small watermark, which Pro removes. The defaults already produce something worth posting; everything after that is you shaping it to fit your idea.
About.p3: Speed and control, more than anything else. Speed, because the gap between an idea and a posted video is where most content dies; if a clip takes twenty minutes and three apps, you stop making clips. Control, because reposted content does not grow an account. When you set the mode, the colours, the pacing and the hook yourself, the video is yours and it stands a real chance in a feed that has seen every recycled clip.
About.p4: We also care about staying out of your way. The simulator updates as you change things, so you learn by doing rather than reading a manual. Settings have plain names. The hard part, the physics and the rendering, happens quietly in the background while you focus on whether the video is fun to watch.
About.p5: Your work stays with you. Presets and settings live in your browser and videos render on your own machine, not on a server we control. We are not interested in harvesting your data or locking your creations behind an account. The less we know about you, the better the tool feels to use. The details are in our <privacy>privacy policy</privacy>.
About.p6: {siteName} is a small, independent project rather than a venture-backed company with a roadmap full of upsells, and that shapes what gets built. New modes and settings appear because creators ask for them. When you write in through the <feedback>feedback page</feedback>, the note reaches the person actually working on the tool, and a lot of what is in the simulator today exists because someone asked for it.
About.p7: The plan is to keep the core free and keep adding modes, effects and quality-of-life touches that make a good clip faster to build. If you make something with it, that is the whole point. Go make a ball smash through some walls.
About.toolP1: {siteName} is a browser tool for making the bouncing-ball videos that fill TikTok, Reels and YouTube Shorts. Pick a mode, adjust a few settings and watch it play – all free, with no account, no installation and no video editor involved. When a clip is ready, record it and download it – free videos carry a small watermark, Pro exports them clean; everything happens in the tab you already have open, so an idea becomes a finished video in a couple of minutes.
About.toolP2: The format works because it is simple. A ball bounces inside a ring with a gap. Every time it slips through, something pays off: a wall shatters, the ball multiplies, colour floods the screen, a target is hit. Viewers want to know how it ends, so they keep watching. That small loop of tension and release is what drives the views, and here you control every part of it instead of reposting someone else's clip.
About.tweakP: The look is yours. Add rings for a longer build-up or remove them for a fast payoff. Turn on rainbow walls, switch the break effect between confetti, shatter and shockwave, or stack all three. Add spikes for danger, glow for polish and a colour trail so fast motion looks deliberate. Put your own image on the ball, write a hook like "will it escape?" across the top and load a melody so the bounces land on a beat. Small changes matter: one extra ring can be the difference between a clip people skip and one they watch twice.
About.exportP: When the run looks right, record it in the browser and export a video sized for vertical feeds. No screen-capture app and no re-encoding elsewhere; on Free the video carries a small watermark, which Pro removes. Found a combination you like? Save it as a preset and reuse it for a whole series; many accounts post the same mode every day with small variations.

Desktop.privacyBody: Everything runs on your PC. The local AI works offline; a cloud key you enter is stored encrypted on your PC and only sent to the provider you chose. The app only goes online to download a model you asked for and to check GitHub for updates.

privacy.title: Payments
privacy.content: Pro is paid through the provider you choose – Stripe, PayPal or NOWPayments – on its own checkout page and under its own privacy policy; your card or wallet details never reach us. Our billing server keeps what it needs to issue, renew and restore your licence: your email, the plan, and the provider's payment or subscription reference. The licence itself is a signed key stored in your browser.

terms.title: Pro subscriptions
terms.content: Playing with the simulator and recording or exporting videos is free; videos made without a Pro licence carry a watermark. Pro – $10 a month or $79 a year – exports them without the watermark and adds publishing to your accounts. Card and PayPal subscriptions renew automatically until you cancel them (in Stripe's customer portal or your PayPal account); a crypto payment buys a prepaid period of 30 or 365 days that does not renew. A licence stays valid until the end of the period paid for.

FightLeague.fighter_thor: God of thunder: swings his hammer, throws it at the nearest foe and calls it back, then strikes every foe with lightning.
FightLeague.fighter_loki: The trickster: four daggers orbit him and fly one by one; Illusion conjures two decoys that soak up the hits.
FightLeague.fighter_spiderman: Quick and slippery: web shots slow the foe they stick to, and Web Trap holds the nearest foe for two seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_ironman: Repulsor blasts at the nearest foe on a steady cadence; the Unibeam fires a wide ray for a second.
FightLeague.fighter_captainamerica: His shield blocks hits from the front and flies at the foe every few seconds; Shield Ricochet bounces it between every foe.
FightLeague.fighter_hulk: Big, slow and heavy: every punch hurts and knocks the foe away, and Hulk Smash sends out a shockwave.
FightLeague.fighter_superman: Heat vision: a thin red ray at the nearest foe every two seconds; Solar Flare is a shockwave of heavy damage.
FightLeague.fighter_batman: Batarangs circle him and fly at the foe; Smoke Bomb makes him untouchable for two seconds and his next hit triple.
FightLeague.fighter_joker: Razor cards orbit him and fly one by one; Laughing Gas slows every foe and turns its aim backwards.
FightLeague.fighter_wonderwoman: A sword, and bracelets that block hits from the front; the Lasso of Truth pulls the nearest foe in and holds it.
FightLeague.fighter_mario: Bouncing fireballs that ricochet off a wall once; Super Star makes him invulnerable for three seconds and every touch hurts.
FightLeague.fighter_link: A sword that sweeps a wide arc on every bounce; the Spin Attack whirls it all the way round at double damage.
FightLeague.fighter_samus: Her arm cannon fires a steady stream of shots; the Charge Shot is one huge, slow projectile.
FightLeague.fighter_captainfalcon: Fast fists and a fast car's worth of speed; the Falcon Punch makes his next hit five times as strong.
FightLeague.fighter_littlemac: A blur of very fast, very light jabs; the Star Punch hits four times as hard and freezes the foe for a second.
FightLeague.fighter_sonic: The fastest fighter in the league hits by running into you; the Spin Dash triples his speed and doubles his damage.
FightLeague.fighter_yuumi: Her book fires slow homing bolts; Final Chapter turns its pages into a beam that lasts two seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_katarina: Throws daggers and blinks to every third one she throws; Death Lotus spins a ring of blades around her.
FightLeague.fighter_garen: A broad sword and thick armour; Demacian Justice quadruples his next hit on a foe below half its HP.
FightLeague.fighter_jinx: Her minigun sprays fast, weak bullets; the Super Mega Death Rocket explodes in a shockwave where it lands.
FightLeague.fighter_ahri: Orbs fly out, hit on the way and come back to her; Spirit Rush dashes onto the nearest foe three times.
FightLeague.fighter_ryu: Fists and a slow Hadouken fireball; the Shoryuken triples his next hit and launches the foe.
FightLeague.fighter_ken: Faster fists and a flaming Hadouken; the Shoryureppa makes his next three hits double.
FightLeague.fighter_chunli: Lightning-fast kicks; the Spinning Bird Kick turns her into a ring of kicks for two seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_scorpion: His spear on a chain drags the hit foe to him; Hellfire burns everything around him.
FightLeague.fighter_subzero: Ice shots freeze the foe they hit for a second; the Ice Clone freezes whoever touches it.
FightLeague.fighter_masterchief: A burst rifle, three shots a trigger; the Spartan Charge rushes in and triples his next hit.
FightLeague.fighter_doomslayer: A shotgun cone of pellets at close range; the BFG fires a wide green beam.
FightLeague.fighter_kratos: The Blades of Chaos whirl on their chains; Spartan Rage doubles his damage and heals 20 HP over three seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_steve: A diamond sword; TNT drops a block that explodes in a shockwave after a one-second fuse.
FightLeague.fighter_pikachu: Short electric arcs at any foe in range; Thunderbolt strikes every foe with lightning.
FightLeague.fighter_charizard: Breathes a cone of fire ahead; Blast Burn sets the ground around him ablaze.
FightLeague.fighter_goku: Fists and ki blasts; the Kamehameha is a blue beam that lasts more than a second.
FightLeague.fighter_vegeta: Fists and ki blasts; Final Flash takes longer to charge and fires a wider beam.
FightLeague.fighter_naruto: Shuriken orbit him and fly one by one; Shadow Clone summons two clones that fight for four seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_sasuke: A quick blade; Chidori blinks onto the nearest foe four times in a row.
FightLeague.fighter_luffy: Rubber fists that reach across half the ring; the Gum-Gum Gatling punches four times as fast for two seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_saitama: One slow punch at triple damage; the Serious Punch is worth half of the foe's maximum HP.
FightLeague.fighter_luke: A green energy blade; the Force Push throws every foe across the ring.
FightLeague.fighter_vader: A red blade, slower and stronger; the Force Choke holds the nearest foe for two seconds and hurts it.
FightLeague.fighter_yoda: Tiny and fast with a short green blade; Force Lift holds the nearest foe up for two seconds, then slams it.
FightLeague.fighter_maul: A double-bladed saber, a blade at both ends; the Saber Throw flies at the foe and comes back.
FightLeague.fighter_harrypotter: Fast bolts from his wand; Expelliarmus disarms the nearest foe for three seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_voldemort: Stronger, slower bolts; Avada Kedavra is one unblockable bolt at five times the damage.
FightLeague.fighter_gandalf: A staff of homing orbs and a sword; You Shall Not Pass makes him untouchable and pins every foe to the far wall.
FightLeague.fighter_legolas: The fastest bow in the league; Arrow Storm looses twelve arrows at once.
FightLeague.fighter_godzilla: A long tail sweeping behind him; Atomic Breath is a blue beam.
FightLeague.fighter_kingkong: Slow, heavy fists; the Chest Beat doubles his damage and knockback for three seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_alien: Claws in front and a tail behind; Acid Blood burns every attacker for four seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_predator: A shoulder plasma caster and wrist blades; Cloak makes him invulnerable and untargetable.
FightLeague.fighter_johnwick: Precise pistols; Baba Yaga makes his next five shots double and homing.
FightLeague.fighter_neo: Fast martial arts; Bullet Time slows every foe and every shot to a crawl while he moves at full speed.
FightLeague.fighter_terminator: A shotgun and a lot of armour; the Minigun fires twelve bullets at once.
FightLeague.fighter_robocop: The Auto-9 fires three-round bursts; Targeting makes his next nine shots home in.
FightLeague.fighter_homelander: Laser eyes and fists; the Laser Sweep holds a red beam for a second and a half.
FightLeague.fighter_omniman: Heavy fists; the Viltrumite Rush triples his speed and doubles his damage for two seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_aang: Airbending pushes that knock foes away but barely hurt; the Avatar State is a ring of fire and a bolt of lightning.
FightLeague.fighter_zuko: Firebending: a cone of fire ahead; Lightning Redirect fires a crackling beam.
FightLeague.fighter_jonsnow: A longsword; Ghost, his white wolf, joins the fight for four seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_nightking: Throws slow, heavy ice spears; Raise the Dead summons three wights for four seconds.
FightLeague.fighter_gerald: Our own ball headbutts its way through the league; Mega Bounce doubles its speed and damage for three seconds.
